question.text: If the function $f(x) = \dfrac{2^{5x}}{k}$ has an inverse function given by $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{\log_2{(7x)}}{5},$ what is the value of $k?$
question.explanation:
To find $f^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y\mathbin{:}$
\begin{align} y &= \dfrac{2^{5x}}{k} \end{align}

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives \begin{align} x &= \dfrac{2^{5y}}{k}. \end{align}

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

\begin{align} x &= \dfrac{2^{5y}}{k} \\[5pt] kx &= 2^{5y} \\[5pt] 2^{5y} &= kx \\[5pt] \log_2{\left(2^{5y}\right)} &= \log_2 {(kx)} \\[5pt] 5y &= \log_2 {(kx)} \\[5pt] y &= \dfrac{\log_2{(kx)}}{5} \end{align}

Therefore, the inverse function is $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{\log_2 {(kx)}}{5}.$

Comparing our answer with the given expression, we conclude that $k=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{7}.$

question.text: The inverse of the function $f(x) = e^{3x}$ is $f^{-1}(x) =$
question.explanation:
To find $f^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} y &= e^{3x} \end{align}

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives \begin{align} x &= e^{3y}. \end{align}

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

\begin{align} x &= e^{3y} \\[5pt] \ln{x} &= \ln\big(e^{3y}\big) \\[5pt] \ln{x} &= 3y \\[5pt] 3y &= \ln{x} \\[5pt] y &= \dfrac{\ln{x}}{3} \end{align}

Therefore, the inverse function is $f^{-1}(x) =\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\ln{x}}{3}}.$

question.text: The inverse of the function $f(x) = \dfrac12\cdot 4^{3x}-5$ is
question.explanation:
To find $f^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} y &= \dfrac12\cdot 4^{3x}-5 \end{align}

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives \begin{align} x &= \dfrac12\cdot 4^{3y}-5. \end{align}

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

\begin{align} x &=\dfrac12\cdot 4^{3y}-5\\[5pt] \dfrac12\cdot 4^{3y} &= x + 5 \\[5pt] 4^{3y} &= 2x +10 \\[5pt] \log_4{\left(4^{3y}\right)} &=\log_4{(2x + 10)} \\[5pt] 3y &= \log_4{(2x + 10)} \\[5pt] y &=\dfrac{1}{3} \log_4{(2x + 10)} \end{align}

Therefore, the inverse function is $f^{-1}(x) =\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{3} \log_4{(2x + 10)}}.$

question.text: The inverse of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{7}\cdot 8^{5x-2} $ is
question.explanation:
To find $f^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align} y &= \dfrac{1}{7}\cdot 8^{5x-2} \end{align}

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives \begin{align} x &= \dfrac{1}{7}\cdot 8^{5y-2} . \end{align}

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows: \begin{align} x &= \dfrac{1}{7}\cdot 8^{5y-2} \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{7}\cdot 8^{5y-2} &= x \\[5pt] 8^{5y-2} &= 7x \\[5pt] \log_8{\left(8^{5y-2}\right)} &= \log_8{(7x)} \\[5pt] 5y-2 &= \log_8{(7x)} \\[5pt] 5y &= \log_8{(7x)} + 2\\[5pt] y &= \dfrac{\log_8{(7x)} + 2}{5} \end{align}

Therefore, the inverse function is $f^{-1}(x) =\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{ \dfrac{\log_8{(7x)} + 2}{5} }.$

question.text: The inverse of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}\log_2(x) + \dfrac{1}{2}$ is $f^{-1}(x) =$
question.explanation:
To find $f^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align} y &=\dfrac{1}{2}\log_2(x) + \dfrac{1}{2} \end{align}

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives \begin{align} x &= \dfrac{1}{2}\log_2(y) + \dfrac{1}{2}. \end{align}

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

\begin{align} x &= \dfrac{1}{2}\log_2(y) + \dfrac{1}{2}\\[5pt] x - \dfrac{1}{2} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\log_2{y}\\[5pt] 2x - 1 &= \log_2{y}\\[5pt] 2^{2x - 1} &= 2^{\log_2{y}} \\[5pt] 2^{2x - 1} &= y \\[5pt] y &= 2^{2x - 1} \end{align}

Therefore, the inverse function is $f^{-1}(x) = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{2^{2x - 1}}.$

question.text: The inverse of the function $f(x) = \log_7\left(x+4\right)$ is $f^{-1}(x) =$
question.explanation:
To find $f^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align} y &= \log_7\left(x+4\right) \end{align}

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives \begin{align} x &= \log_7\left(y+4\right). \end{align}

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:
\begin{align} x &= \log_7(y+4) \\[5pt] 7^x &= 7^{\log_7(y+4)} \\[5pt] 7^x &= y+4 \\[5pt] y &= 7^x - 4 \end{align}

Therefore, the inverse function is $f^{-1}(x) = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{7^x - 4}.$

example.title: Finding Inverses of Logarithmic Functions With More Than Two Transformations

question.text:
If the function $f(x) =3\log_2\left(\dfrac{x-1}{3}\right) - k?$ has an inverse function given by
\[
f^{-1}(x) = 3\cdot 2^{(x+6)/3}+1,
\]
what is the value of $k?$
question.explanation:
To find $f^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y\mathbin{:}$
\begin{align} y = 3\log_2\left(\dfrac{x-1}{3}\right) - k \end{align}

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives \begin{align} x = 3\log_2\left(\dfrac{y-1}{3}\right) - k. \end{align}

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows: \begin{align} x &= 3\log_2\left(\dfrac{y-1}{3}\right) - k\\[5pt] 3\log_2\left(\dfrac{y-1}{3}\right) &= x+k\\[5pt] \log_2\left(\dfrac{y-1}{3}\right) &= \dfrac{x+k}{3} \\[5pt] 2^{\log_2\left( (y-1)/3 \right)} &= 2^{(x+k)/3} \\[5pt] \dfrac{y-1}{3} &= 2^{(x+k)/3} \\[5pt] y-1 &= 3\cdot 2^{(x+k)/3} \\[5pt] y &= 3\cdot 2^{(x+k)/3}+1 \end{align}

Therefore, the inverse function is $f^{-1}(x) = 3\cdot 2^{(x+k)/3}+1.$

Comparing our answer with the given expression, we conclude that $k = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{6}.$

example.title: Finding Inverses of Logarithmic Functions With More Than Two Transformations

question.text: The function $f(x) =4\ln(kx-3)+1$ has an inverse function given by $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot e^{(x-1)/4}+1.$ What is the value of $k?$
question.explanation:
To find $f^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} y &= 4\ln(kx-3)+1 \end{align}

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives \begin{align} x &= 4\ln(ky-3)+1. \end{align}

We make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

\begin{align} x &= 4\ln(ky-3)+1 \\[5pt] 4\ln(ky-3) &= x-1 \\[5pt] \ln(ky-3) &= \dfrac{x-1}{4} \\[5pt] e^{\ln(ky-3)} &= e^{(x-1)/4} \\[5pt] ky-3 &= e^{(x-1)/4} \\[5pt] ky &= e^{(x-1)/4}+3 \\[5pt] y &= \dfrac{1}{k}\left( e^{(x-1)/4}+3 \right) \\[5pt] y &= \dfrac{1}{k} \cdot e^{(x-1)/4} +\dfrac{3}{k} \end{align}

Therefore, the inverse function is $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{1}{k} \cdot e^{(x-1)/4}+\dfrac{3}{k}.$

Comparing our answer with the given expression, we conclude that $k=3.$
